transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Sofia Alvarez (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Celestis Head of ML), Priya Singh (Platform Eng), Noah Rivera (CTO), Asha Kapoor (SRE)

Summary (auto): Customer is building low-latency inference for trading signals; main asks are p95 under 90-120ms for short responses, ability to sustain 200 concurrent streams during market open bursts, and token/sec benchmarking for 2k token prompts with streaming. Security requirements include SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS/HSM and VPC/private deployment options.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, i'm the account owner. we also have Ethan and Sofia from our SE team. how's it going?
[00:08] Liam: hey thanks, uh brief intro — i'm liam, head of ml at celestis, we run real-time signal generation across equities and fx, trying to avoid long tails during market open.
[00:18] Priya: hi i'm priya, platform eng we own infra for inference.
[00:24] Noah: noah here CTO, quick blocker is latency p95 and predictable cost.
[00:29] Maya: great, main agenda is latency and throughput — p95 targets, concurrency, streaming behavior, and figure out hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[00:36] Ethan: quick question to start: what are your p95 SLO targets and what does a typical response look like? (token length, streaming, etc)
[00:44] Liam: target p95 is sub 120ms for our short template responses, most are ~100-200 tokens, but we also have longer eval flows up to 2k tokens where p95 can be more relaxed to ~1s, major pain is the 30-minute market open bursts where concurrency spikes from 50 to ~200 concurrent requests.
[00:58] Asha: also need streaming so we can start showing partial tokens to downstream systems, that reduces overall perceived latency.
[01:08] Ethan: got it. are you currently hosting models yourselves or using any hosted provider?
[01:12] Priya: currently we have a mixed setup — some on-prem for sensitive workflows and some on cloud VMs, we also trialled a hosted provider but ran into jitter at scale during bursts.
[01:21] Sophia (misattributed): we saw — we saw some queuing in the other provider — (laughs)
[01:27] Maya: okay, a couple of clarifying Qs: are the burst patterns predictable (market open / close) and can you tolerate short queuing during peaks?
[01:36] Liam: predictable yes, but tolerance is very low, maybe up to 200ms queuing at worst — but p95 should still be sub 120ms ideally.
[01:45] Ethan: for sub-120ms p95 on 100-200 token responses we usually recommend Dedicated with pinned capacity and low-latency GPUs. Hosted can work if you accept multi-tenant latency guarantees and slightly higher variance.
[01:58] Noah: packed question: what about streaming — does Redwood support early-token streaming and how does that affect p95 and throughput?
[02:06] Sofia: yes we support streaming with chunked token emission and function calling too. streaming reduces perceived latency because you get first tokens earlier; for p95 on end-to-end completion, streaming often reduces the tail but network and client side assembly matters.
[02:20] Priya: curious about token/sec benchmarking — we need numbers for both single request token/sec and aggregate throughput for 200 concurent streams.
[02:29] Ethan: we typically measure tokens/sec per GPU for a given model/sequence length, and then factor in batching and continuous KV cache savings. for example, a quantized 13B on our optimized runtime can do ~400-800 token/sec per GPU depending on sequence and kernel paths; but that depends a lot on chunk sizes and whether you enable 4-bit quantization.
[02:47] Liam: hmm can we get a table of expected token/sec for the model families we mentioned — and what about p95 under burst?
[02:56] Maya: yes we'll include a benchmarking plan. quick note on dedicated: you can pin instances to keep KV caches warm which dramatically lowers p95 for repeated prefixes — that helps if many requests share prompt prefixes.
[03:08] Asha: do you have prefix caching or KV caching? we've seen other vendors talk about KV cache but in practice it's inconsistent.
[03:16] Ethan: we have KV cache + prefix cache; runtime maintains cache per model shard and we can configure sticky routing so high-QPS clients are sent to warmed pools. caveat — if traffic is highly spiky you need reserved capacity or burst capacity to avoid cold starts.
[03:30] [03:30] Liam: and what about autoscaling latency? if we scale up during open, how long is spin-up?
[03:35] Sofia: autoscale spin-up depends on deployment type — Dedicated autoscale can spin extra GPUs in minutes depending on infra, but cold-starting a private on-prem host might take longer. for critical flows we recommend reserved capacity with burst buffer.
[03:48] Noah: security — we need SOC2, SSO/SAML, RBAC and KMS integration — also we may need VPC/private deployment for some models. how mature is Redwood in those areas?
[03:58] Maya: we are SOC2 compliant, support SSO/SAML, RBAC via console, and integrate with KMS/HSM for key management. Private deployments (VPC & on-prem) are available for enterprise customers, and you can bring your own key in private.
[04:12] Priya: great. licensing and pricing — curious about committed Reserved Dedicated pricing vs on-demand hosted.
[04:19] Maya: we'll share a pricing sheet. short version: hosted is usage-based (per-token), Dedicated is reserved with monthly/annual commits and offers predictability. there are also burst buffers for short spikes.
[04:34] [04:34] Liam: on the technical front, we need an initial benchmark plan: sample prompt set, p95 and median targets, concurrency profile (baseline and burst), and whether streaming or full completion measurement.
[04:44] Ethan: propose: 1) you supply 50 representative prompts (mix short 100-200 tokens and long 2k tokens), 2) we run baseline throughput tests on Hosted and Dedicated emulations, 3) run 1-hour burst tests simulating market open to measure p95 and queueing. we'll provide token/sec and latency curves.
[04:59] Priya: how do you simulate our network conditions? we have private peering and low-latency links between our infra and cloud region.
[05:06] Sofia: we can run tests from your VPC (for Private) or from our Hosted in the same cloud region; for Dedicated we can co-locate in region and include network RTT in measurements. note that public hosted has slightly more network variance.
[05:18] Liam: any tips on prompt engineering that reduces latency? e.g., shorter prefixes, using streaming, function calling minimal payloads.
[05:25] Ethan: yep, suggestions: minimize prompt length when possible, canonicalize repeated prefixes so KV cache helps, use streaming to get first token earlier, and consider model distillation / smaller family for time-sensitive flows. we also recommend batching small parallel requests into multi-request pipelines where feasible.
[05:39] Asha: what's your recommendation for 200 concurrent streams at market open — Dedicated pool size? 
[05:44] Ethan: rough calc: if a live 13B does ~500 token/sec on our optimized runtime and each short response is 150 tokens, that's ~0.3s of compute per request (compute only). to sustain 200 concurrent streams with p95 under 120ms you'd need pinned capacity and likely 6-8 GPUs depending on exact model and kernel, plus burst buffer. this is a ballpark; we need to run a benchmark with your exact prompts to size properly.
[06:09] Noah: can you explain how batching affects p95? i've seen batching improve throughput but increase tail latency for single-request p95.
[06:16] Ethan: right — batching increases throughput by amortizing kernel overhead, but introduces queueing if you wait to gather a batch. our runtime uses continuous batching to reduce this — it tries to form small batches quickly to avoid long wait times. Dedicated can be tuned for lower batching pause times at the cost of some throughput efficiency.
[06:33] Liam: can we get a failover plan? if Dedicated pool is saturated, what's fallback?
[06:38] Maya: you can configure smart routing — requests fall back to compatible model variants in hosted or other regions; you can also configure graceful degradation (e.g., shorter response length or quicker timeouts). we'll document recommended fallbacks in the pilot plan.
[06:52] Priya: are there any gotchas with token accounting for streaming? our billing model needs clarity.
[06:58] Maya: billing counts tokens processed; streaming doesn't change token accounting, but if you stream partial tokens and then cancel it early, we count tokens generated. we'll include sample billing scenarios in the pricing docs.
[07:09] [07:09] Ethan: on benchmarking methodology — we'll capture median and p95, token/sec, GPU utilization, and end-to-end network RTT. we'll also surface distribution plots so you can see tail behavior.
[07:20] Asha: one more Q on KV cache warm-up — how long to warm and how much memory footprint?
[07:26] Sofia: warming depends on prompt variety; for repeated prefixes warm-up is fast (seconds to minutes), memory footprint scales with kv size and sequence length. we'll include estimated memory per model in the benchmark doc.
[07:38] Liam: timeline — we want a pilot within 2 weeks and production readiness in 8-10 weeks if benchmarks look good.
[07:45] Maya: sounds reasonable. immediate next steps: we'll send pricing and dedicated configs, Ethan will draft a benchmark plan, and we'll schedule the deep-dive with your SREs.
[07:55] Noah: on legal/compliance, we'll want an NDA and SOC2 report; can you share those?
[08:01] Maya: yes, will send SOC2 attestation and standard enterprise NDA.
[08:06] Priya: any competitor notes we should be aware of? we tested other providers and saw high variance during peaks and less transparency on kernel/runtime choices.
[08:16] Ethan: we try to be transparent about runtime profiles and quantization tradeoffs so you can make informed choices.
[08:23] Liam: ok wrapping up — recap?
[08:26] Maya: recap: 1) Celestis needs sub-120ms p95 for short responses, 200 concurrent burst, streaming enabled, security incl SOC2/SSO/KMS, 2) Redwood to provide Dedicated config + pricing, benchmarking plan, and schedule deep-dive, 3) Celestis to share prompt set and access for tests, 4) target pilot in 2 weeks.
[08:46] Ethan: i'll follow up with a benchmarking timeline and exact infra requirements (region, GPUs, VPC peering notes).
[08:54] Sofia: i'll prepare a short streaming demo and SDK snippet to show partial token handling and client assembly best practices.
[09:02] Liam: thanks everyone, we'll get the prompt set over by monday.
[09:07] Maya: thanks all, talk soon.

(End of transcript)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attributions (Sophia/Sofia), minor word substitutions e.g., "KV cash" instead of "KV cache" in auto text, filler words preserved.
